segments.text: American Fork City Council — Truth in Taxation Public Hearing — August 23, 2022:
American Fork City Council — Regular Session — August 23, 2022:

entities.speaker: David H. Bunker
entities.remark-context: Police demand and proposed property-tax increase

segments.text: At the Truth in Taxation hearing, City Administrator David Bunker said demand for police services had risen 46.6% over five years. He identified increased public-safety services as one reason for the proposed tax increase and said service levels would decline without additional revenue.

After hearing public comment on the proposed tax increase, Mayor Bradley Frost said the city could not continue providing public safety in the same manner it had in the past and said the council would consider the testimony before voting.

entities.speaker: David H. Bunker
entities.remark-context: Station 52 shooting range and construction contract

segments.text: City Administrator David Bunker explained that eliminating the Station 52 shooting range would save approximately $1.04 million, while leaving it unfinished would save approximately $693,000. He recommended proceeding with the amended construction contract while allowing staff to identify value-engineering savings.
Mayor Bradley Frost supported including the Station 52 shooting range, saying it was important for the city to have and control that asset.

Council Member Clark Taylor said public safety was a top priority and cautioned that reducing construction costs could cost more later. He supported providing high-quality facilities that matched what the city expected from public-safety personnel.

entities.speaker: Robert E. Shelton
entities.remark-context: Cedar Hills contract and Station 52 costs

segments.text: Council Member Robert Shelton asked how much additional annual revenue the Cedar Hills public-safety contract would provide after Station 52 opened and said he hoped it would offset part of the facility’s cost. City Administrator David Bunker estimated approximately $300,000, before an additional fee after the city vacated Cedar Hills’ building.

entities.speaker: Kevin J. Barnes
entities.remark-context: Shooting-range design and police facility funding

segments.text: Council Member Kevin Barnes asked why the shooting range was no longer planned for the basement and, after hearing that police and fire impact-fee funds each held approximately $2.5 million, asked why the city should not also build the police station. Staff recommended completing Station 52 first.

entities.label: Police-service demand and the proposed property-tax increase

segments.text: At the public hearing, the city presented police-service demand and public-safety staffing as central reasons for increasing property-tax revenue. The mayor closed by stating that the prior level of public-safety service could not continue unchanged.
Relevant passages from the official meeting minutes:

Mr. Bunker explained why the city would consider a tax increase. There have been increases in public safety services and the cost of road improvements that are driving the need for additional revenue. As the general fund expenses grows over time, the value of the dollar and what can be done with that dollar decreases due to inflation and the city had less revenue to provide the same level of service. The demand for police services has risen 46.6% in the past five years, and fire/rescue service costs have risen 69%. As a side note, Mr. Bunker stated Station 51 was the busiest fire station in Utah County. The cost of street construction materials has increased 17.5% in the last year alone, and since 2010 road construction costs have increased an astounding 44%. In other words, the city can do less road improvements today with the same amount of dollars that we could have done in 2008.

Mr. Bunker stated that without additional revenue, the city will go backwards in the level of service.

Mr. Bunker stated some city departments have not increased personnel for decades. The city is growing, and we still have to provide services to all the residents. There have been additional personnel specifically in public safety, due to large call volumes.

Mayor Frost vouched that they have elected officials that care for the community and all kind of people, from the fixed income to the affluent income. As a council, they will ponder on everything said tonight and take it into consideration. He stated that the Council does care for the residents and the communities. He mentioned that the city cannot continue to provide public safety in the manner the city has done in the past. He thanked everyone who was here tonight and happy to engage with the residents.

entities.label: Station 52 shooting range and police-facility funding

segments.text: The council weighed the cost, safety, ownership, and timing of a police shooting range within the Station 52 project and discussed whether available police impact fees should instead advance a police-station project.
Key points written for this site:

• City Administrator David Bunker presented the construction cost and options to omit or defer completion of the shooting range.
• Mayor Bradley Frost supported retaining the range, while council members discussed construction quality, public-safety priorities, Cedar Hills revenue, safety, and whether police impact fees should also advance a police station.
• The council approved the amended construction contract, including the range, while authorizing staff to pursue value-engineering savings; Council Member Ryan Hunter abstained.

contents.label: Read the complete relevant minutes passage

segments.text:
Mr. Bunker reported that back in October 2020, American Fork city entered in a contract with SIRQ construction to build Fire Station 52. At that time, there were a lot of unknowns, specifically the guaranteed maximum price. As they did not have set plants, SIRQ could not go out and secure pricing for construction. As the city did not have property yet for the station, they were looking at a couple of sites in that vicinity. Now, the property has been secured and we are ready to move forward with construction. SIRQ has gone through and received bids from various sub-contractors. Within that, the city looked into the process with Value Engineering of certain items and there is a potential for some savings up to $150,000 to $300,000. Before the council was a cost estimate for the fire station. Mr. Bunker then went over the where the revenues will come from and where the costs are for Station 52.

He explained the revenue was from the 2019 bond proceeds, police impact fees, and police impact fees. The total cost of the project is $11,590,311, which was higher than anticipated due to inflation and the price of the land. He noted the fire station will be constructed to the minimum footprint for fire but would include a shooting range on the west side of the station. There were a couple of options that would bring the cost down a bit. Those were to not fully finish the shooting range for a savings of $692,784 or to not building the shoot range for a savings of $1,038,120. Mr. Bunker did not feel the prices would get an cheaper than they are today, so if they did not construct or complete the shooting range they would have to bring in a contractor in the future.

Mr. Bunker recommended to amend the CMGC with SIRQ construction in the amount of $9,112,335 and allow staff to work on Value Engineering items that would reduce costs.

Mayor Frost expressed appreciation for the summary and agreed, especially the shooting range. He felt it was important to have that asset and control in the city. Mayor Frost asked the council if they had any questions.

Council Member Carroll commented on Value Engineering. She expressed that she fully supports Value Engineering and wanted to make the fire station has high quality construction, looks nice, and will last a long time. She wasn’t sure if Value Engineering reduces that quality, but it was her concern.

Council Member Taylor commented the city was conscious of the cost, however, there have been times where in the end it costs more money down the road. He added that with public safety being a number one priority, as elected officials, he agreed with Council Member Carroll that the city have state of the art things that makes sense. In terms of all things that will serve the public, that the city works to provide that which we expect of our public safety and hoped that the budget is right where it needs to be.

Council Member Shelton asked about the contract with Cedar Hills and what the city would increase annually by having our station built. Mr. Bunker estimated that it was close to $300,000 but that there would be an additional fee when the city vacates the Cedar Hills building.

Council Member Shelton hopes that it will help offset some of the fees. He mentioned in the contract section 6.1.5, where it talks about rental rates for construction management, it says N/A in there and wanted to double check that it was supposed to be there. Mr. Bunker replied that it was not applicable.

Council Member Barnes commented he thought the firing range was going to be in the basement of the fire department and wanted to know why that was no longer an option. Mr. Bunker responded that one of the reasons was cost. It is more expensive to be done in the basement than build it out on the side. Another concern was safety if there was a stray bullet it could harm someone above.

Council Member Barnes inquired about the Impact Fees and how much was in it. Mr. Bunker responded that it was about $2.5 million in each one. Council Member Barnes asked why the city shouldn’t do the police station also if we have the money. Mr. Bunker replied that staff recommends completing the fire station project first.

Council Member Hunter mentioned that discussions about the fire station happened prior before he was on the council, and he is working for the contractor and wanted to abstain from voting.

Council Member Shelton moved to approve the AMENDED CMGC Contract with SIRQ Construction for Fire Station 52 with a guaranteed maximum price of $9,112,335 (or other GMP if shooting range is modified or eliminated) and instruct staff to coordinate the consideration of value engineering items which will reduce the GMP accordingly. Council Member Taylor seconded the motion. Voting was as follows:
RESULT: APPROVED [UNANIMOUS]
MOVER: Rob Shelton, Council Member
SECONDER: Clark Taylor, Council Member
AYES: Shelton, Carroll, Barnes, Taylor
ABSTAIN: Ryan Hunter
